title: Answering Islam on the Trinity

keyTerms.d: The absolute, indivisible oneness of God at the center of Islam: God is one in essence, one in will, one in worship; He has no peer, no partner, no offspring, no internal composition. A zeal for the oneness of God that is sincere and that a Christian should meet with respect.

The gravest sin in Islamic theology — associating anything with God, setting up a partner alongside the Creator or ascribing divinity to a creature. As the Qur'an describes it, shirk is the elevation of something outside God — an idol, a prophet, a saint — to a rank alongside Him. The Trinity adds nothing to God from outside, so it is not the shirk the objection fears.

The “trinity” the Qur'an actually names and rejects — taking “me and my mother as deities besides Allah.” No Christian creed, council or catechism has ever placed Mary in the Godhead — not Catholic, not Orthodox, not Protestant — so whatever 5:116 rejects, it is not the doctrine the Church confesses.

Two Arabic words for “son.” Walad connotes a biological child, the fruit of procreation; ibn can be used far more broadly and figuratively. The Qur'an denies God has a walad (112:3; 19:35) — a procreated child Christians deny too — while Arabic-speaking Christians have customarily called Christ ibn Allāh, Son in the relational, non-physical sense.

What the Creed means by “begotten”: the Son is “begotten, not made” — not created in time, not the product of any act, but eternally derived from the Father, sharing the one undivided essence. Athanasius insisted this generation is timeless and non-physical. So the popular “how can God have a son?” rests on a picture of sonship — biological, temporal — that Nicene Christianity also rejects.

Settling the Mihna, mainstream Sunni orthodoxy held God's inner speech eternal and uncreated — an attribute that is, in the Ash'aris' own formula, “neither He nor other than He”: not identical with the bare essence, yet not a separate thing beside it. It is an attribute, not a Person who knows and loves, and it cannot become incarnate.

Not a word-match (kalima is not kalam, and a well-read Muslim corrects that in one sentence) but a structural point: settling the Mihna, Ash'ari/Maturidi orthodoxy built the very category it tells Christians is incoherent — something eternal and uncreated that is genuinely God's without being a second god. The asymmetry is decisive: their formula denies otherness, while John positively confesses the Word IS God, a divine person and not an attribute. Scoped to mainstream Ash'ari Sunnism, not Islam as such — a serious consideration, not a knock-down proof.

The doctrine actually under dispute: one God, the Father Almighty; one Lord Jesus Christ, of one substance (homoousios) with the Father; the Holy Spirit, the giver of life. Three persons (hypostaseis), one being (ousia) — not three gods who cooperate, and not one God wearing three masks in turn (modalism). Numerically one in essence, eternally three in personal relation.

derive.q: Surah 5:116 names the rejected trinity as God, Jesus, and Mary — and no creed, council or catechism has ever placed Mary in the Godhead. So the target of that verse is…?
derive.ans: a doctrine the Church condemns too — not the one it confesses
derive.why: Whatever Surah 5:116 is rejecting, it is not the doctrine the Church confesses. A refutation of a position nobody holds refutes nobody. The honest Christian answer is an emphatic no — and we condemn that idea as you do.

derive.q: The Qur'an denies God has a walad — a procreated biological child — while the Creed's “begotten” means eternal, non-physical generation. So on the walad denial, Christian and Muslim…?
derive.ans: agree — the popular objection aims at a sonship Nicaea also rejects
derive.why: The denial of a walad rejects physical, procreated offspring, and Christians agree without reservation; that idea is pagan and foreign to the Gospel. “Begotten” in the Creed is an eternal relation within the Godhead, not an event in a divine biography — so the question rests on a picture of sonship, biological and temporal, that Nicene Christianity also rejects.

derive.q: Shirk is elevating something outside God to a rank alongside Him. The Trinity adds nothing to God from outside and places no second being beside Him. So the Trinity is…?
derive.ans: not shirk — a claim about God's inner life, not a partner added
derive.why: The Trinity is not the association of a creature with the Creator; it is a claim about what the one God eternally is in His own inner life — an eternal communion of Father, Son and Spirit in a single undivided essence. Nor does the Christian call a creature God: the eternal Son took a complete human nature without ceasing to be God. So the answer to the charge is no.

derive.q: Settling the Mihna, mainstream Sunni orthodoxy held God's speech eternal and uncreated — an attribute “neither He nor other than He.” So the premise that the One admits no internal distinction is…?
derive.ans: contested even within Islam — not a self-evident axiom
derive.why: To quote “God is one” against the Trinity presupposes that “one” excludes triune relation, which is the very thing in dispute. Once the Ash'ari allowance of real, eternal distinction of some kind within the one undivided God is granted, “the One can admit no internal distinction at all” is no longer Islam's settled possession; it is a contested premise.

derive.q: Grant all of it — the parallel takes away the sweeping charge. Does it, by itself, prove the Trinity?
derive.ans: no — an attribute is not a Person; it clears the charge, it does not prove the doctrine
derive.why: The disanalogy is real and must be conceded: these attributes are not persons who know, will and love one another, and they cannot become incarnate; so the parallel is partial, and it is not on its own evidence for three persons. What it does is remove the sweeping form of the objection — that any eternal Word alongside God must be a second deity. The positive case rests on revelation and on the historical case for who Jesus was.

honestState.p1: The strong, essentially undisputed part: the Qur'an's explicit anti-Trinitarian statements — the God-Jesus-Mary triad of 5:116, the “three gods” of 5:73, the denial of a procreated walad — target a doctrine the Church condemns as heresy, and Christians can agree gladly that those would be false. The genuinely contested part is the hinge: whether “distinct eternal attribute” and “distinct eternal person” are near enough in structure for the one to illuminate the other. That is a serious consideration, not a knock-down proof — an attribute is not a Person, and that gap is the whole disagreement.
honestState.fairness: The refined objection is held by serious people — classical theologians in the tradition of al-Ghazali and the Ash'ari school, and contemporary Muslim philosophers — and many Muslim theologians, with some Western scholars of kalam, hold the attribute/person disanalogy decisive enough to dissolve the parallel entirely. The scope must be stated honestly: this bites against mainstream Ash'ari/Maturidi Sunnism, not Islam as such. The Athari/Salafi school (following Ibn Taymiyya) will say you are cross-examining theologians rather than Islam — a fair correction — and the Mu'tazila, whose created-Qur'an doctrine lives on in Twelver and Zaydi Shi'i theology, reject the Ash'ari resolution outright. On the text, the Notre Dame Islamicist Gabriel Said Reynolds reads 5:116 largely rhetorically. Neither side has produced a knock-down proof of the metaphysics, and honesty requires saying so.
honestState.verdict: The explicit anti-Trinitarian verses do not reach the doctrine the Church confesses, so on those the answer is plainly no — and we reject them too. The one objection that does reach Nicaea — that the One can admit no internal distinction — rests on a premise that is contested rather than proven, and contested even within Islam's own debate over the divine attributes; so it does not, as it stands, refute the Trinity. The Trinity is not the shirk the objection fears. This clears the charge against it; it does not prove the doctrine. What we hold true — one God, eternally Father, Son and Holy Spirit — rests finally on revelation and on the historical case for who Jesus was.

order: The Qur'an's explicit anti-Trinity polemic targets a doctrine Christians do not hold — a God-Jesus-Mary triad of separate gods (5:116, 5:73) — which Nicene Christianity condemns as firmly as Islam does.

The premise the deeper objection rests on — that the divine One admits no internal distinction whatever — is contested inside Islamic theology itself (Ash'ari orthodoxy holds God's attributes eternal and uncreated, “neither He nor other than He”); that is not a version of the Trinity, for an attribute is not a Person.

Therefore the explicit verses do not reach the doctrine the Church confesses, and the one objection that does reach Nicaea rests on a contested premise — so the Trinity is not the shirk the objection fears; this clears the charge, it does not prove the doctrine, which rests on revelation and the resurrection.

cards.q: State Premise 1 — and its precision check.
cards.a: The Qur'an's explicit anti-Trinity polemic targets a doctrine Christians do not hold: “Say not Three” (4:171) alongside taking “Jesus and his mother as gods besides Allah” (5:116) — a God-Jesus-Mary triad of separate gods, which Nicene Christianity condemns as firmly as Islam does. Precision: it does not say the Qur'an has no quarrel with Christians — it denies what we do confess, that Jesus is God (5:72), and that, not the caricature, is the real disagreement.

cards.q: State Premise 2 — and its precision check.
cards.a: The premise the deeper objection rests on — that the divine One admits no internal distinction whatever — is contested inside Islamic theology itself: Ash'ari orthodoxy holds God's attributes eternal and uncreated, “neither He nor other than He.” Precision: that is not a version of the Trinity, and we should not pretend it is — those attributes are not persons who know and love one another, and they cannot become incarnate. The narrow point and no more: internal distinction in the one God is not unthinkable on Islam's own terms.

cards.q: What does the conclusion reach — and not reach?
cards.a: That the explicit anti-Trinitarian verses do not reach the doctrine the Church confesses — on those, plainly no, and we reject them too — and that the one objection which does reach Nicaea rests on a premise contested rather than proven. So the Trinity is not the shirk the objection fears. It does not, by itself, prove the Trinity; the positive case rests on revelation and the resurrection. It clears the charge.

cards.q: What “trinity” does the Qur'an actually condemn at 5:116?
cards.a: God, Jesus AND MARY taken as deities besides Allah — a triad with Mary in the Godhead, which no Christian creed, council or catechism has ever held, in any tradition. A refutation of a position nobody holds refutes nobody. But 5:72 also denies what we do confess — that Jesus is God — and that is the real disagreement.

cards.q: The walad objection — what does the Creed's “begotten” actually mean?
cards.a: The Qur'an denies God has a walad, a procreated biological child — which Christians deny too; that idea is pagan and foreign to the Gospel. “Begotten” in the Creed means eternal generation: the Son eternally from the Father, begotten not made, never created in time, sharing the one undivided essence. The popular “how can God have a son?” rests on a picture of sonship — biological, temporal — that Nicene Christianity also rejects.

cards.q: Reply to: the Trinity is shirk.
cards.a: Shirk is elevating something outside God — a creature, prophet or saint — to a rank alongside Him. The Trinity adds nothing to God from outside and places no second being beside Him; it describes what the one God eternally IS — an eternal communion of Father, Son and Spirit in a single undivided essence. Nor does the Christian call a creature God: the eternal Son took a complete human nature without ceasing to be God. So the answer is no: the Trinity is not the shirk the objection fears.

cards.q: Two versions of the Eternal Word argument — which one holds, and why not the other?
cards.a: Run it STRUCTURALLY, never lexically. The lexical version — “the Qur'an is God's eternal Word, the Qur'an calls Jesus God's Word, therefore Jesus is eternal” — equivocates between kalam nafsi (God's eternal inner speech) and the kalima of 4:171, and a Muslim who knows the terms corrects it in one sentence. Structurally: settling the Mihna, Ash'ari/Maturidi orthodoxy built the very category it calls incoherent — something eternal and uncreated genuinely God's without being a second god. Still not the Trinity: an attribute is not a Person, and that gap is the whole disagreement.

cards.q: Reply to: “Word just means the command Be! — Jesus was created by it like Adam.”
cards.a: 4:171 calls Jesus HIS WORD — a title given to him, not a description of how he was made; Adam, made by the very same command, never receives it, and no one else in the Qur'an does. So “like Adam” (3:59) is a comparison about origin without a human father; it does not explain why only one of the two is named the Word of God. Keep it off the lexical bridge — the narrow point is enough: the title is unique, and the kun-reading explains how he came to be, not why only he bears it.

cards.q: Reply to: “Allah's attributes are eternal without being persons — problem solved.”
cards.a: Look at what the formula concedes: God's speech is eternal and uncreated, and Ash'ari theology declines to flatten it into the bare essence. No Muslim concedes the point, and we should not say they do — but as a matter of logic, mainstream Sunni doctrine of the attributes cannot sustain the sweeping version of the objection, that any eternal Word alongside God must be a second deity. It is NOT a version of the Trinity: an attribute is not a Person, and that gap is the whole disagreement, not a difference of wording.

cards.q: Reply to the hardest objection — the refined tawhid charge that the One cannot be complex.
cards.a: Concede first: this is the real disagreement, a genuine metaphysical dispute argued by able philosophers on both sides, not a mere confusion. Then reply: the objection assumes divine oneness MUST mean undifferentiated simplicity — but that assumption is the point in dispute; it is asserted by tawhid, not demonstrated by it. Once the Ash'ari allowance of real, eternal distinction within the one God is granted, “the One can admit no internal distinction at all” is a contested premise, not Islam's settled possession. And “a creature called God” misdescribes the Incarnation: the eternal Son took a complete human nature without ceasing to be God. So it does not, as it stands, refute the Trinity.

cards.q: Reply to: “you're cross-examining Sunni theologians, not Islam.”
cards.a: Grant it plainly: the uncreated-Qur'an doctrine is Ash'ari and Hanbali doctrine, not a Qur'anic verse, and the argument never needed the Qur'an to be uncreated or the lexical bridge. What it needed was only this: that mainstream Islamic orthodoxy, working from its own tawhid, concluded God's attributes are eternal and uncreated — which shows eternal distinction within the one God is not unthinkable on Islam's own terms. An attribute is still not a Person, and that gap is the whole disagreement. But the objection can no longer simply be presumed.

cards.q: Does this argument call a creature God — and does it prove the Trinity?
cards.a: No on both. The Christian does not call a creature God: the eternal Son took a complete human nature to himself without ceasing to be God — fully God and fully man, two natures in one person. And the argument does not prove the Trinity; it clears the charge against it. The positive case rests on revelation and on the historical case for who Jesus was — whether he said and did what only God can, and was vindicated by resurrection.

obj.q: The Trinity is shirk — three divine beings worshiped where there should be one, a man and even a woman exalted to the rank of God. It is the one unforgivable sin.
obj.model: Shirk, as the Qur'an describes it, is the elevation of something outside God — an idol, a prophet, a saint — to a rank alongside God. The Qur'an brings this charge against Christians (5:72) because it takes Jesus to be a creature raised to God's rank. But the Trinity adds nothing to God from outside; it places no second being beside Him. Nor does the Christian call a creature God: the eternal Son took a complete human nature to himself without ceasing to be God. It is a claim about what the one God eternally is in His own inner life — not a bare, solitary monad, but an eternal communion of Father, Son and Spirit in a single undivided essence. Whether that claim is true is the live question; but it is a claim about God's interior life, not about adding partners — and that distinction is the hinge of the whole conversation. So the answer to the charge is no: the Trinity is not the shirk the objection fears.

obj.q: Grant everything — that you do not worship Mary, that you mean one essence and three persons not three gods, that “begotten” means eternal generation. You still introduce real distinction into the One whose very perfection is to be undivided and simple, and still call a man — Jesus of Nazareth, who ate and wept and died — God. The deepest meaning of tawhid is that God is utterly unique, without internal composition. The Trinity, however carefully you state it, makes the Absolute complex — and that is shirk in its most refined and dangerous form.
obj.model: First, the concession. The Muslim is right that this is the real disagreement, and right that it is not a mere confusion. Whether the divine unity can be triune — whether perfect oneness is compatible with real internal relation — is a genuine metaphysical dispute, argued by able philosophers on both sides, and it is not settled by quoting a verse or a creed. Second, the reply. The objection assumes that divine oneness must mean absolute, undifferentiated simplicity — that any internal distinction is automatically a division. But that assumption is exactly the point in dispute; it is asserted by tawhid, not demonstrated by it. Once the Ash'ari allowance of real, eternal distinction of some kind within the one undivided God is granted, “the One can have no internal distinction at all” is no longer Islam's settled possession; it is a contested premise. And “a creature called God” misdescribes the Incarnation: the eternal Son took a complete human nature to himself without ceasing to be God — fully God and fully man, two natures in one person. So the one objection which does reach Nicaea rests on a premise contested rather than proven, and contested even within Islam's own debate over the divine attributes — so it does not, as it stands, refute the Trinity. This does not prove the Trinity; the positive case rests on revelation and on the historical case for who Jesus was.

obj.q: The uncreated Qur'an is an attribute, not a person. The Ash'ari eternal Word (kalam) is not a distinct hypostasis who knows, loves, and can be addressed. The Christian Son is a person — one who can say “I,” who prays to the Father, who became incarnate. And for us the attribute/person distinction was the whole point from the start, not a concession forced out under pressure — it is decisive enough to dissolve your parallel entirely.
obj.model: This is correct as far as it goes. The categories are genuinely different, and any honest account must concede the difference: the eternal kalam nafsi is not a Trinitarian person, and to claim Islam secretly teaches the Trinity would be both false and unfair. But notice what the reply concedes in order to work. It concedes that Ash'ari theology affirms an eternal, uncreated, really-distinct divine reality that is “neither He nor other than He” — and then argues this is acceptable because it is an attribute rather than a person. The defense, in other words, is not that an eternal Word-with-God is impossible; the defense is that this particular eternal Word happens not to be personal. That is a far narrower claim. Grant it. Then the objection to Christ must be restated as “a distinct eternal person in God would be a second god” — and that premise is asserted by tawhid, not demonstrated by it; it is exactly the point in dispute. So the charge that an eternal Word alongside God must mean two gods is one mainstream Sunni theology does not sustain, because it affirms exactly such a Word. This argument does not prove the Trinity; it clears the charge against it.

obj.q: Nothing in the Qur'an says God's speech is uncreated — that is later Ash'ari and Hanbali speculation. You are cross-examining a school of theology and calling it Islam; Qur'anic Islam owes you nothing here.
obj.model: The fact is worth granting plainly: the uncreated-Qur'an doctrine is Ash'ari and Hanbali doctrine, not a Qur'anic verse, and a Muslim is entitled to say so. But notice what our argument actually needed. It never needed the Qur'an to be uncreated, and it never needed the lexical bridge — which equivocates between kalam nafsi, God's eternal inner speech, and the kalima of 4:171, an utterance. What it needed was only this: that mainstream Islamic orthodoxy, working from its own doctrine of tawhid, concluded that God's attributes are eternal and uncreated. Whatever else that establishes, it establishes that eternal distinction within the one God is not unthinkable on Islam's own terms. An attribute is still not a Person, and that gap is the whole disagreement. But the objection can no longer simply be presumed.

unseen.q: But we both believe in one God — isn't this just a dispute about words? The same God under different labels, with Christians adding complications Muslims leave off.
unseen.model: Here we have to be honest in both directions, and false comfort would help no one. Yes — both of us are monotheists in the numerical sense: we bow before one Creator, not many, and that agreement is a real on-ramp, a place two people can genuinely reason together. But it is an on-ramp, not a shared doctrine of God, and I would be misleading you to call it one. It is not that our two accounts of God are the same, or equally adequate, or that the disagreement is small. Whether the one God is triune, and who Jesus is, is precisely the question still dividing us — a genuine difference, not a merely verbal one, and not the same God wearing two labels. So I will not tell you we worship the same God under different names; I will say we agree there is one God, not many, and then part, honestly and deeply, over what that one God is. That is a disagreement worth having slowly, with the texts open — and it turns finally on the real question, the one with a phantom doctrine cleared out of the way: who is Jesus?
